Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Local page replacement vs Global page replacement in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Local page replacement is choosing a victim only from the process own frames; Global page replacement is choosing a victim from all frames.

Main differences:
- Isolation: Local page replacement - isolates processes; Global page replacement - lets processes affect each other.
- Throughput: Local page replacement - may underuse memory; Global page replacement - usually gives better throughput.
- Predictability: Local page replacement - is more predictable; Global page replacement - is less predictable.

Conclusion: Global gives better throughput and local gives predictability.

Question: When would you choose Deadlock detection over Deadlock avoidance?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Deadlock detection when deadlocks are rare.

Simple explanation: Deadlock detection is letting deadlock happen and then finding it. On overhead, Deadlock detection - has overhead during periodic checks, whereas Deadlock avoidance - has constant overhead.

Example:
If deadlocks are rare, then Deadlock detection is the better fit than Deadlock avoidance.

Question: What is Physical Address in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: A physical address is the actual location in main memory.

Simple explanation: It is produced by the MMU after translating the logical address.

Example:
Logical address 200 may become physical address 4200.

Question: When would you choose SSTF over FCFS disk scheduling?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose SSTF when you want less head movement.

Simple explanation: SSTF is a disk algorithm serving the nearest request first. On fairness, SSTF - may starve far requests, whereas FCFS disk scheduling - is fair.

Example:
If you want less head movement, then SSTF is the better fit than FCFS disk scheduling.

Question: Why is Compaction important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It solves external fragmentation.

Definition: Compaction is the process of moving allocated memory blocks together to create one large free block.

Example:
Moving three processes to the start of memory merges scattered holes into one large hole.

Question: What is the difference between Many-to-one thread model and One-to-one thread model?
Answer:
Short answer: Many-to-one thread model is mapping many user threads to one kernel thread, while One-to-one thread model is mapping each user thread to a kernel thread.

Key differences:
- Parallelism: Many-to-one thread model - has no parallelism; One-to-one thread model - has full parallelism.
- Blocking: Many-to-one thread model - blocks all threads; One-to-one thread model - blocks only one thread.
- Overhead: Many-to-one thread model - has low overhead; One-to-one thread model - has higher overhead.

Question: Which is better, Process context switch or Thread context switch?
Answer:
Verdict: Thread switches are cheaper.

Simple explanation: Cost: Process context switch - is more expensive; Thread context switch - is cheaper. Memory: Process context switch - changes the address space; Thread context switch - keeps the same address space.

Example:
Choose Process context switch when you switch between programs. Choose Thread context switch when you switch within an application.

Question: Explain First Come First Served (FCFS) with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: It uses a simple queue: the process that arrives first gets the CPU first and runs until it finishes.

Example:
If P1 (24 ms) arrives before P2 (3 ms), P2 must wait 24 ms even though it is short.

Key point: FCFS is a scheduling algorithm that runs processes in the order they arrive.

Question: Which is better, Process or Thread?
Answer:
Verdict: Neither is universally better: use threads for speed and shared data, and processes for safety and isolation.

Simple explanation: Memory: Process - has its own separate memory; Thread - shares memory with other threads of the same process. Creation cost: Process - is heavy to create and switch; Thread - is light to create and switch.

Example:
Choose Process when you need strong isolation between tasks. Choose Thread when you need fast, cooperating tasks that share data.

Question: When would you choose Multiprogramming over Multitasking?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Multiprogramming when the aim is throughput in batch systems.

Simple explanation: Multiprogramming is keeping several programs in memory to keep the CPU busy. On goal, Multiprogramming - maximizes CPU utilization, whereas Multitasking - improves responsiveness and interactivity.

Example:
If the aim is throughput in batch systems, then Multiprogramming is the better fit than Multitasking.

Question: What is the difference between Symmetric multiprocessing and Asymmetric multiprocessing?
Answer:
Short answer: Symmetric multiprocessing is a design where all processors share the same tasks and OS, while Asymmetric multiprocessing is a design where one master processor controls the others.

Key differences:
- Control: Symmetric multiprocessing - has no master; Asymmetric multiprocessing - has a master.
- Efficiency: Symmetric multiprocessing - balances load better; Asymmetric multiprocessing - can make the master a bottleneck.
- Complexity: Symmetric multiprocessing - is more complex; Asymmetric multiprocessing - is simpler.

Question: What is the difference between RAID 0 and RAID 1?
Answer:
Short answer: RAID 0 is a RAID level that stripes data across disks, while RAID 1 is a RAID level that mirrors data on two disks.

Key differences:
- Redundancy: RAID 0 - has no redundancy; RAID 1 - has full redundancy.
- Speed: RAID 0 - gives high read and write speed; RAID 1 - gives good reads and normal writes.
- Capacity: RAID 0 - uses the full capacity; RAID 1 - uses half the capacity.

Question: When would you choose Linked allocation over Indexed allocation?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Linked allocation when files are mostly read sequentially.

Simple explanation: Linked allocation is chaining blocks with pointers inside each block. On random access, Linked allocation - is slow, whereas Indexed allocation - is fast.

Example:
If files are mostly read sequentially, then Linked allocation is the better fit than Indexed allocation.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of C-SCAN Algorithm?
Answer:
Limitation: The long return movement adds seek time.

Simple explanation: It treats the cylinders as a circular list and serves requests in one direction only.

Example:
The head sweeps up to the last cylinder, then returns to cylinder 0 and sweeps up again.

Question: Which is better, DMA or Programmed I/O?
Answer:
Verdict: DMA is better for large transfers.

Simple explanation: CPU use: DMA - keeps the CPU free; Programmed I/O - keeps the CPU busy. Speed: DMA - is faster for large data; Programmed I/O - is slower.

Example:
Choose DMA when you transfer large blocks. Choose Programmed I/O when you transfer small amounts of data.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Heap Memory?
Answer:
Limitation: It is slower than the stack and can cause leaks and fragmentation.

Simple explanation: Programs request memory with malloc() or new and must release it, giving flexibility in size and lifetime.

Example:
int *p = malloc(100 * sizeof(int));

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Distributed Operating System?
Answer:
Limitation: It is complex to design and depends on network reliability and security.

Simple explanation: It shares resources, files and processing across machines transparently.

Example:
A cluster that spreads tasks across many nodes behaves as one system to users.

Question: What is the difference between API and System call?
Answer:
Short answer: API is a set of functions for programmers, while System call is a direct request to the kernel.

Key differences:
- Level: API - is a higher level; System call - is a lower level.
- Portability: API - is more portable; System call - is OS-specific.
- Example: API - POSIX API; System call - read().

Question: When would you choose C-SCAN over SCAN?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose C-SCAN when you want uniform waiting under heavy load.

Simple explanation: C-SCAN is a disk algorithm that sweeps in one direction and jumps back. On wait time, C-SCAN - gives more uniform wait times, whereas SCAN - gives uneven wait times.

Example:
If you want uniform waiting under heavy load, then C-SCAN is the better fit than SCAN.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Inode?
Answer:
Limitation: The number of inodes is fixed at creation, so a disk can run out of inodes even with free space.

Simple explanation: It records owner, permissions, size, timestamps and block addresses, but not the file name.

Example:
Running ls -i shows the inode number of each file.

Question: Why is Zombie Process important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: Knowing about it helps prevent process table exhaustion.

Definition: A zombie process is a process that has finished execution but still has an entry in the process table.

Example:
If a parent never calls wait(), its dead child stays as a zombie shown as Z in ps.

Question: What is Address Binding in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: Address binding is the process of mapping program addresses to physical memory addresses.

Simple explanation: Binding can happen at compile time, load time or execution time.

Example:
A compiler may assign a variable the logical address 100 which is mapped to 5100 in RAM at run time.

Question: Explain CPU Burst and I/O Burst with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: Processes alternate between the two, and scheduling decisions use burst behaviour.

Example:
A video encoder has long CPU bursts, while a text editor has short CPU bursts and long I/O waits.

Key point: A CPU burst is the time a process spends executing on the CPU and an I/O burst is the time spent waiting for I/O.

Question: When would you choose RAID 1 over RAID 0?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose RAID 1 when you need safety of data.

Simple explanation: RAID 1 is a RAID level that mirrors data on two disks. On speed, RAID 1 - gives good reads and normal writes, whereas RAID 0 - gives high read and write speed.

Example:
If you need safety of data, then RAID 1 is the better fit than RAID 0.

Question: What is Critical Section in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: A critical section is a part of code that accesses shared resources and must not be run by more than one process at a time.

Simple explanation: If two processes enter it together, shared data may become inconsistent, so the OS or programmer must allow only one at a time.

Example:
Code that increments a shared counter is a critical section.

Question: When would you choose Mutex over Spinlock?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Mutex when the lock may be held for long.

Simple explanation: Mutex is a lock that puts waiting threads to sleep. On best for, Mutex - works well for longer waits, whereas Spinlock - works well for very short waits.

Example:
If the lock may be held for long, then Mutex is the better fit than Spinlock.

Question: What is the difference between Multitasking and Multithreading?
Answer:
Short answer: Multitasking is running multiple tasks or processes concurrently, while Multithreading is running multiple threads inside one process.

Key differences:
- Unit: Multitasking - works with processes; Multithreading - works with threads.
- Resources: Multitasking - has separate resources per task; Multithreading - shares resources among threads.
- Overhead: Multitasking - has higher switching overhead; Multithreading - has lower switching overhead.

Question: When would you choose Thread over Process?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Thread when you need fast, cooperating tasks that share data.

Simple explanation: Thread is a lightweight unit of execution inside a process. On creation cost, Thread - is light to create and switch, whereas Process - is heavy to create and switch.

Example:
If you need fast, cooperating tasks that share data, then Thread is the better fit than Process.

Question: Compare Round Robin and Priority scheduling.
Answer:
Definition: Round Robin is a scheduler that gives equal time slices to all processes. Priority scheduling is a scheduler that runs the highest-priority process first.

Simple explanation: They differ mainly in fairness, starvation and tuning. Fairness: Round Robin - treats all processes equally; Priority scheduling - favours important processes.

Example:
Choose Round Robin when you want equal sharing of the CPU. Choose Priority scheduling when some tasks are more important than others.

Question: What is File Permissions in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: File permissions define who can read, write or execute a file.

Simple explanation: In Unix they are set for owner, group and others as r, w and x bits.

Example:
chmod 755 file gives the owner full access and others read and execute.

Question: What is the difference between Long-term scheduler and Short-term scheduler?
Answer:
Short answer: Long-term scheduler is the scheduler that admits jobs into memory, while Short-term scheduler is the scheduler that selects the next process for the CPU.

Key differences:
- Frequency: Long-term scheduler - runs rarely; Short-term scheduler - runs very often.
- Role: Long-term scheduler - controls the degree of multiprogramming; Short-term scheduler - selects the CPU process.
- Speed: Long-term scheduler - can be slow; Short-term scheduler - must be very fast.

Question: Compare Logical address and Physical address.
Answer:
Definition: Logical address is an address generated by the CPU. Physical address is an address in main memory.

Simple explanation: They differ mainly in visibility, generation and range. Visibility: Logical address - is seen by the program; Physical address - is seen by the memory unit.

Example:
Choose Logical address when you write or debug a program. Choose Physical address when you analyse real memory use.

Question: Explain Throughput and CPU Utilization with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: A good scheduler keeps the CPU busy and completes many jobs.

Example:
Finishing 20 jobs per minute while the CPU is 95 percent busy indicates efficient scheduling.

Key point: Throughput is the number of processes completed per unit time, and CPU utilization is the percentage of time the CPU is busy.

Question: When would you choose Standard page table over Inverted page table?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Standard page table when you want fast lookups.

Simple explanation: Standard page table is a table with one entry per page. On search, Standard page table - is faster, whereas Inverted page table - is slower and needs hashing.

Example:
If you want fast lookups, then Standard page table is the better fit than Inverted page table.

Question: Why is Paging important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It removes external fragmentation and simplifies memory allocation.

Definition: Paging is a memory management scheme that divides memory into fixed-size blocks called pages and frames.

Example:
A 12 KB process with 4 KB pages needs 3 pages that can sit in any 3 free frames.

Question: What is the difference between Zombie process and Orphan process?
Answer:
Short answer: Zombie process is a finished process whose exit status is not yet collected, while Orphan process is a running process whose parent has ended.

Key differences:
- State: Zombie process - is already terminated; Orphan process - is still running.
- Cause: Zombie process - parent has not called wait(); Orphan process - parent has terminated.
- Cleanup: Zombie process - is removed when the parent reads status; Orphan process - is adopted by init.

Question: What is exec() System Call in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: exec() replaces the current process image with a new program.

Simple explanation: The process keeps its PID but its code, data and stack are replaced by the new program.

Example:
A shell calls fork() and then exec() in the child to run a command.

Question: Why is Virtual Machine important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It gives isolation, easy testing and better hardware utilization.

Definition: A virtual machine (VM) is a software emulation of a computer that runs its own OS.

Example:
You can run Linux inside a VM on a Windows laptop.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Authentication vs Authorization in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Authentication is verifying who you are; Authorization is deciding what you may do.

Main differences:
- Question: Authentication - asks who you are; Authorization - asks what you can access.
- Order: Authentication - comes first; Authorization - comes after authentication.
- Example: Authentication - login with password; Authorization - file permissions.

Conclusion: Both are required for security.

Question: What is the difference between Process context switch and Thread context switch?
Answer:
Short answer: Process context switch is switching between processes, while Thread context switch is switching between threads of the same process.

Key differences:
- Cost: Process context switch - is more expensive; Thread context switch - is cheaper.
- Memory: Process context switch - changes the address space; Thread context switch - keeps the same address space.
- TLB: Process context switch - may flush the TLB; Thread context switch - keeps TLB valid.

Question: Compare Hard real-time system and Soft real-time system.
Answer:
Definition: Hard real-time system is a system where missing a deadline is a failure. Soft real-time system is a system where missing a deadline reduces quality.

Simple explanation: They differ mainly in deadline, example and cost. Deadline: Hard real-time system - must always be met; Soft real-time system - can occasionally be missed.

Example:
Choose Hard real-time system when failure may cause harm. Choose Soft real-time system when small delays are acceptable.

Question: Why is Disk Structure and Seek Time important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: Reducing it is the goal of disk scheduling.

Definition: Seek time is the time the disk head takes to move to the required track.

Example:
Moving the head from track 10 to track 200 takes much more time than from 10 to 12.

Question: Which is better, Contiguous allocation or Linked allocation?
Answer:
Verdict: Linked allocation is better for flexible file sizes, and contiguous allocation is better for speed.

Simple explanation: Access: Contiguous allocation - supports fast direct access; Linked allocation - supports only slow sequential access. Fragmentation: Contiguous allocation - suffers external fragmentation; Linked allocation - has no external fragmentation.

Example:
Choose Contiguous allocation when you need fast access to fixed-size files. Choose Linked allocation when files grow often and are read sequentially.

Question: Why is Authentication important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It is the first line of defence against unauthorized access.

Definition: Authentication is the process of verifying the identity of a user or process.

Example:
Logging in with a username and password authenticates you.

Question: Why is Shared Memory important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It is the fastest IPC method because the kernel is not involved after setup.

Definition: Shared memory is an IPC method where multiple processes access the same region of memory.

Example:
Two processes map the same segment and one writes results that the other reads.

Question: In an interview, how would you explain Solid State Drive (SSD) to a beginner?
Answer:
Definition: An SSD is a storage device that uses flash memory with no moving parts.

Simple explanation: It reads and writes data electronically, making it much faster than a hard disk.

Why it matters: It gives fast access, low power use and shock resistance.

Example:
Replacing an HDD with an SSD makes boot time much shorter.

Question: Compare Daemon and Regular process.
Answer:
Definition: Daemon is a background service process. Regular process is a user-started foreground process.

Simple explanation: They differ mainly in interaction, lifetime and start. Interaction: Daemon - has no interaction; Regular process - may interact.

Example:
Choose Daemon when you need background services. Choose Regular process when you run a user task.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Android vs iOS in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Android is an open-source mobile OS based on Linux; iOS is a closed mobile OS from Apple.

Main differences:
- Customization: Android - is more customizable; iOS - is less customizable.
- Devices: Android - runs on many vendors; iOS - runs on Apple devices.
- Updates: Android - updates vary by vendor; iOS - updates are consistent.

Conclusion: Choice depends on needs.

Question: When would you choose Test-and-set over Peterson's solution?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Test-and-set when you implement real locks.

Simple explanation: Test-and-set is a hardware instruction for locks. On processes, Test-and-set - supports many processes, whereas Peterson's solution - supports two processes.

Example:
If you implement real locks, then Test-and-set is the better fit than Peterson's solution.

Question: Explain Banker's Algorithm with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: Before allocating, it checks whether all processes could still finish in some order given the available resources.

Example:
If granting a request leaves no safe sequence, the request is made to wait.

Key point: The Banker's algorithm is a deadlock avoidance method that grants a resource request only if the system stays in a safe state.

Question: What is the difference between Shell and Kernel?
Answer:
Short answer: Shell is a program that interprets user commands, while Kernel is the core of the OS that controls hardware.

Key differences:
- Role: Shell - is the user interface; Kernel - is the manager of resources.
- Mode: Shell - runs in user mode; Kernel - runs in kernel mode.
- Replaceable: Shell - can be replaced easily; Kernel - is hard to replace.

Question: What is the difference between Preemptive scheduling and Non-preemptive scheduling?
Answer:
Short answer: Preemptive scheduling is a policy where the OS can take the CPU from a running process, while Non-preemptive scheduling is a policy where a process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks.

Key differences:
- Responsiveness: Preemptive scheduling - gives better response time; Non-preemptive scheduling - can give poor response if a long job runs.
- Overhead: Preemptive scheduling - has more context-switch overhead; Non-preemptive scheduling - has less overhead and is simpler.
- Shared data: Preemptive scheduling - can cause race conditions on shared data; Non-preemptive scheduling - has fewer synchronization issues.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Monitor vs Semaphore in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Monitor is a high-level construct with built-in mutual exclusion; Semaphore is a low-level counter with wait and signal.

Main differences:
- Ease of use: Monitor - is easier and safer; Semaphore - is error-prone.
- Support: Monitor - needs language support; Semaphore - is available in the OS.
- Mutual exclusion: Monitor - is automatic; Semaphore - must be programmed.

Conclusion: Monitors are better for safe code and semaphores give low-level control.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize LRU page replacement vs Optimal page replacement in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: LRU page replacement is an algorithm that evicts the page unused for the longest past time; Optimal page replacement is an algorithm that evicts the page not needed for the longest future time.

Main differences:
- Knowledge: LRU page replacement - uses past history; Optimal page replacement - needs future knowledge.
- Practicality: LRU page replacement - can be implemented; Optimal page replacement - cannot be implemented in real systems.
- Page faults: LRU page replacement - gives near-optimal faults; Optimal page replacement - gives the minimum possible faults.

Conclusion: Optimal is best in theory but LRU is the best practical choice.

Question: When would you choose SSD over HDD?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose SSD when you need speed.

Simple explanation: SSD is a storage device using flash memory. On speed, SSD - is much faster, whereas HDD - is slower.

Example:
If you need speed, then SSD is the better fit than HDD.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Peterson's Solution?
Answer:
Limitation: It works only for two processes and may fail on modern CPUs without memory barriers.

Simple explanation: It uses a flag array and a turn variable so that only one process enters the critical section.

Example:
Each process sets flag[i] = true and turn = j, then waits while the other is interested and has the turn.

Question: When would you choose Mandatory access control over Discretionary access control?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Mandatory access control when you need high security.

Simple explanation: Mandatory access control is access decided by system policy. On flexibility, Mandatory access control - is strict, whereas Discretionary access control - is flexible.

Example:
If you need high security, then Mandatory access control is the better fit than Discretionary access control.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Hybrid Kernel?
Answer:
Limitation: It inherits some complexity and risk from both designs.

Simple explanation: It keeps some services in kernel mode for speed while structuring others in a modular way.

Example:
Windows NT and macOS use hybrid kernels.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Single-level paging vs Multilevel paging in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Single-level paging is using one page table; Multilevel paging is using page tables in several levels.

Main differences:
- Memory use: Single-level paging - uses large tables; Multilevel paging - uses less memory for sparse spaces.
- Lookups: Single-level paging - needs one memory access; Multilevel paging - needs several accesses.
- Scalability: Single-level paging - does not scale; Multilevel paging - scales to big address spaces.

Conclusion: Multilevel paging is better for large address spaces.

Question: Why is Shell important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It gives power users automation through scripts and quick control.

Definition: A shell is a program that provides a command-line or text interface to the operating system.

Example:
Bash is a popular shell on Linux.

Question: What is Turnaround Time and Waiting Time in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: Turnaround time is the total time from process arrival to completion, and waiting time is the time spent in the ready queue.

Simple explanation: Turnaround time = completion time minus arrival time, and waiting time = turnaround time minus burst time.

Example:
A process arriving at 0 with burst 5 that finishes at 12 has turnaround 12 and waiting 7.

Question: What is Virtual Machine in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: A virtual machine (VM) is a software emulation of a computer that runs its own OS.

Simple explanation: A hypervisor divides physical hardware into isolated virtual machines.

Example:
You can run Linux inside a VM on a Windows laptop.

Question: What is C-SCAN Algorithm in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: C-SCAN moves the head in one direction only, and after reaching the end jumps back to the start without serving on the return.

Simple explanation: It treats the cylinders as a circular list and serves requests in one direction only.

Example:
The head sweeps up to the last cylinder, then returns to cylinder 0 and sweeps up again.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Disk Scheduling?
Answer:
Limitation: Some algorithms can cause starvation for far-away requests.

Simple explanation: It reduces the movement of the disk head to improve throughput.

Example:
With requests at cylinders 98, 183, 37 and 122, the OS orders them to reduce head movement.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Real-Time Operating System (RTOS)?
Answer:
Limitation: It usually offers fewer features and needs careful design to guarantee deadlines.

Simple explanation: It uses predictable scheduling so deadlines are met, and correctness depends on timing as well as results.

Example:
Airbag controllers and industrial robots use an RTOS.

Question: What is Direct Memory Access (DMA) in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: DMA is a technique that allows devices to transfer data directly to or from memory without using the CPU for each byte.

Simple explanation: The CPU sets up the transfer and the DMA controller moves the block, then raises an interrupt when done.

Example:
Reading a large file from disk uses DMA to place data into RAM.

Question: Compare Cache memory and Main memory.
Answer:
Definition: Cache memory is a small, fast memory near the CPU. Main memory is the large memory that holds running programs.

Simple explanation: They differ mainly in speed, size and cost. Speed: Cache memory - is much faster; Main memory - is slower.

Example:
Choose Cache memory when you want to speed up frequent accesses. Choose Main memory when you need large storage for programs.

Question: Which is better, Virtual machine or Container?
Answer:
Verdict: Containers are better for efficiency and VMs are better for isolation.

Simple explanation: Size: Virtual machine - is heavy; Container - is lightweight. Start time: Virtual machine - takes minutes; Container - takes seconds.

Example:
Choose Virtual machine when you need different operating systems or strong isolation. Choose Container when you need fast, light deployment.

Question: Compare Fixed partitioning and Variable partitioning.
Answer:
Definition: Fixed partitioning is dividing memory into fixed-size parts. Variable partitioning is dividing memory based on process sizes.

Simple explanation: They differ mainly in fragmentation, flexibility and complexity. Fragmentation: Fixed partitioning - has internal fragmentation; Variable partitioning - has external fragmentation.

Example:
Choose Fixed partitioning when processes are of known sizes. Choose Variable partitioning when process sizes vary.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Process Control Block (PCB)?
Answer:
Limitation: PCBs consume kernel memory, and maintaining many of them adds overhead.

Simple explanation: It holds the process ID, state, program counter, CPU registers, scheduling info, memory limits and open files.

Example:
On a context switch the OS saves the running process state into its PCB and loads another process PCB.

Question: Which is better, Paging or Segmentation?
Answer:
Verdict: Paging is usually preferred in modern systems because it avoids external fragmentation, often combined with segmentation.

Simple explanation: Block size: Paging - uses equal-sized blocks; Segmentation - uses variable-sized segments. Fragmentation: Paging - has internal fragmentation; Segmentation - has external fragmentation.

Example:
Choose Paging when you want simple allocation without external fragmentation. Choose Segmentation when you want protection and sharing at a logical level.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Paging vs Segmentation in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Paging is a memory scheme that uses fixed-size pages; Segmentation is a memory scheme that uses variable-size logical segments.

Main differences:
- Block size: Paging - uses equal-sized blocks; Segmentation - uses variable-sized segments.
- Fragmentation: Paging - has internal fragmentation; Segmentation - has external fragmentation.
- Programmer view: Paging - is invisible to the programmer; Segmentation - matches the logical view of the program.

Conclusion: Paging is usually preferred in modern systems because it avoids external fragmentation, often combined with segmentation.

Question: Which is better, BIOS or UEFI?
Answer:
Verdict: UEFI is better and is replacing BIOS.

Simple explanation: Boot speed: BIOS - is slower; UEFI - is faster. Disk support: BIOS - supports MBR and disks up to 2 TB; UEFI - supports GPT and large disks.

Example:
Choose BIOS when you use old hardware. Choose UEFI when you use modern hardware.

Question: Why is Preemption important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It improves responsiveness and prevents one process from monopolizing the CPU.

Definition: Preemption is the ability of the OS to forcibly take the CPU away from a running process.

Example:
If a high-priority process becomes ready, the OS pauses the current one immediately.

Question: What is Inverted Page Table in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: An inverted page table has one entry per physical frame rather than per virtual page.

Simple explanation: Each entry stores which process and page occupy that frame.

Example:
A 64-bit system with large virtual space can use it to keep the table small.

Question: Why is Memory-Mapped I/O important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It simplifies programming because no special I/O instructions are needed.

Definition: Memory-mapped I/O maps device registers into the memory address space so they can be accessed with normal memory instructions.

Example:
Writing to a certain address may send a byte to a serial port.

Question: Explain Mounting with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: The OS attaches a device file system to a mount point so its files appear under that directory.

Example:
mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/usb makes a USB drive available at /mnt/usb.

Key point: Mounting is the process of making a file system accessible at a directory in the file tree.

Question: Which is better, Peterson's solution or Test-and-set?
Answer:
Verdict: Hardware atomic instructions are better in practice.

Simple explanation: Type: Peterson's solution - is software; Test-and-set - is hardware. Processes: Peterson's solution - supports two processes; Test-and-set - supports many processes.

Example:
Choose Peterson's solution when you learn the theory. Choose Test-and-set when you implement real locks.

Question: Explain Convoy Effect with an example.

One 100 ms job makes five 2 ms jobs wait 100 ms.

Question: When would you choose Physical address over Logical address?
Answer:

If you analyse real memory use, then Physical address is the better fit than Logical address.

Question: Explain Page Fault with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: The OS pauses the process, loads the page from disk into a free frame, updates the page table and restarts the instruction.

Example:
Accessing an array element on a page that is still on disk causes a page fault.

Key point: A page fault occurs when a program accesses a page that is not currently in physical memory.

Question: What is Swapping in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: Swapping is moving a process between main memory and disk to free RAM.

Simple explanation: The OS moves an idle process to a swap area and brings it back when it needs to run.

Example:
A background process that has been idle for long is swapped out to make room for an active one.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Thrashing vs Page fault in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Thrashing is too much paging that stops useful work; Page fault is a single missing page event.

Main differences:
- Scope: Thrashing - is a system-wide condition; Page fault - is a single event.
- Cause: Thrashing - is caused by too many processes; Page fault - is caused by accessing a page not in memory.
- Effect: Thrashing - collapses performance; Page fault - costs time for one access.

Conclusion: Page faults are normal and thrashing is a problem.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Page Table Entry?

Limitation: Many entries make the page table large and memory hungry.

Simple explanation: Bits include valid, dirty, referenced and protection bits.

If the valid bit is 0, accessing that page causes a page fault.

Question: When would you choose Message queue over Pipe?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Message queue when you need structured asynchronous messages.

Simple explanation: Message queue is a queue of messages managed by the OS. On persistence, Message queue - can persist in the kernel, whereas Pipe - disappears when closed.

Example:
If you need structured asynchronous messages, then Message queue is the better fit than Pipe.

Question: Compare Ready queue and Waiting queue.
Answer:
Definition: Ready queue is processes ready to run. Waiting queue is processes waiting for an event.

Simple explanation: They differ mainly in state, next step and scheduler. State: Ready queue - holds ready processes; Waiting queue - holds blocked processes.

Example:
Choose Ready queue when you schedule the CPU. Choose Waiting queue when you handle I/O.

Question: What is the difference between Spinlock and Mutex?
Answer:
Short answer: Spinlock is a lock that busy-waits, while Mutex is a lock that puts waiting threads to sleep.

Key differences:
- CPU use: Spinlock - wastes CPU while waiting; Mutex - does not waste CPU while waiting.
- Best for: Spinlock - works well for very short waits; Mutex - works well for longer waits.
- Context switch: Spinlock - avoids context switches; Mutex - involves context switches.

Question: What is the difference between Monitor and Semaphore?
Answer:
Short answer: Monitor is a high-level construct with built-in mutual exclusion, while Semaphore is a low-level counter with wait and signal.

Key differences:
- Ease of use: Monitor - is easier and safer; Semaphore - is error-prone.
- Support: Monitor - needs language support; Semaphore - is available in the OS.
- Mutual exclusion: Monitor - is automatic; Semaphore - must be programmed.

Question: Compare Spooling and Buffering.
Answer:
Definition: Spooling is queuing jobs on disk for a device. Buffering is holding data temporarily in memory.

Simple explanation: They differ mainly in storage, purpose and example. Storage: Spooling - uses disk; Buffering - uses RAM.

Example:
Choose Spooling when many jobs share a slow device. Choose Buffering when producer and consumer speeds differ.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Multilevel queue vs Multilevel feedback queue in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Multilevel queue is separate queues with fixed process assignment; Multilevel feedback queue is a design with queues where processes can move.

Main differences:
- Movement: Multilevel queue - does not allow movement; Multilevel feedback queue - allows movement.
- Flexibility: Multilevel queue - is less flexible; Multilevel feedback queue - is more flexible.
- Starvation: Multilevel queue - can starve low queues; Multilevel feedback queue - can avoid it with aging.

Conclusion: MLFQ is more flexible and more widely used.

Question: Which is better, Windows or Linux?
Answer:
Verdict: Neither is universally best: Windows suits desktops and Linux suits servers and developers.

Example:
Choose Windows when you need broad desktop applications. Choose Linux when you need servers, control or open source.

Question: Explain Journaling with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: The file system writes planned updates to a journal first; after a crash it replays or discards incomplete entries.

Example:
ext4 and NTFS use journaling to recover quickly after a power failure.

Key point: Journaling is a file system technique that logs changes before applying them to the main structures.

Question: What is Optimal Page Replacement in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: The optimal algorithm replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future.

Example:
It evicts the page whose next use is farthest away in the reference string.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Authentication?
Answer:
Limitation: Weak passwords and stolen credentials can bypass it, so multi-factor authentication is advised.

Simple explanation: The system checks credentials such as passwords, tokens or biometrics.

Example:
Logging in with a username and password authenticates you.

Question: What is the difference between ext4 and NTFS?
Answer:
Short answer: ext4 is the default Linux file system, while NTFS is the main Windows file system.

Key differences:
- Platform: ext4 - is native on Linux; NTFS - is native on Windows.
- Features: ext4 - has journaling and extents; NTFS - has journaling and ACLs.
- Compatibility: ext4 - needs drivers on Windows; NTFS - needs drivers on Linux.

Question: What is the difference between Deadlock and Starvation?
Answer:
Short answer: Deadlock is a state where processes wait forever for each other, while Starvation is a state where one process waits indefinitely while others proceed.

Key differences:
- Scope: Deadlock - involves a group of processes all blocked; Starvation - involves one or few processes being ignored.
- System progress: Deadlock - no process in the group can progress; Starvation - the rest of the system continues to work.
- Solution: Deadlock - is solved by prevention, avoidance or detection; Starvation - is solved by aging or fair scheduling.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Cache Memory?
Answer:
Limitation: It is expensive and small, and a cache miss costs extra time.

Simple explanation: When the CPU needs data it checks the cache first; a hit is much faster than reading RAM.

Example:
A loop that reads the same array repeatedly benefits from cached values.

Question: In an interview, how would you explain Demand Paging to a beginner?
Answer:
Definition: Demand paging loads a page into memory only when it is needed.

Simple explanation: A page is brought in from disk on the first access that causes a page fault.

Why it matters: It saves memory and reduces start-up time.

Example:
A large program starts quickly because only its first pages are loaded.

Question: Explain Bounded Waiting with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: It guarantees that a waiting process will eventually get its turn.

Example:
In a fair lock, a thread waits for at most N-1 other threads.

Key point: Bounded waiting means there is a limit on how many times other processes can enter their critical section after a process has requested entry.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Multiprogramming vs Multitasking in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Multiprogramming is keeping several programs in memory to keep the CPU busy; Multitasking is switching rapidly between tasks so they seem to run together.

Main differences:
- Goal: Multiprogramming - maximizes CPU utilization; Multitasking - improves responsiveness and interactivity.
- Switching: Multiprogramming - switches mainly when a program waits for I/O; Multitasking - switches using time slices.
- User view: Multiprogramming - has little interactivity; Multitasking - feels interactive.

Conclusion: Multitasking is better for users because it adds time-sharing on top of multiprogramming.

Question: What is Process Control Block (PCB) in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: A PCB is a data structure the OS keeps for every process to store its information.

Simple explanation: It holds the process ID, state, program counter, CPU registers, scheduling info, memory limits and open files.

Example:
On a context switch the OS saves the running process state into its PCB and loads another process PCB.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize FCFS disk scheduling vs SSTF in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: FCFS disk scheduling is a disk algorithm serving requests in arrival order; SSTF is a disk algorithm serving the nearest request first.

Main differences:
- Seek time: FCFS disk scheduling - has a high total head movement; SSTF - has lower head movement.
- Fairness: FCFS disk scheduling - is fair; SSTF - may starve far requests.
- Complexity: FCFS disk scheduling - is simple; SSTF - needs to compute distances.

Conclusion: SSTF is better for performance, and FCFS is better for fairness.

Question: Why is Direct Memory Access (DMA) important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It frees the CPU for other work during large transfers.

Definition: DMA is a technique that allows devices to transfer data directly to or from memory without using the CPU for each byte.

Example:
Reading a large file from disk uses DMA to place data into RAM.

Question: What is the difference between Paging and Segmentation?
Answer:
Short answer: Paging is a memory scheme that uses fixed-size pages, while Segmentation is a memory scheme that uses variable-size logical segments.

Key differences:
- Block size: Paging - uses equal-sized blocks; Segmentation - uses variable-sized segments.
- Fragmentation: Paging - has internal fragmentation; Segmentation - has external fragmentation.
- Programmer view: Paging - is invisible to the programmer; Segmentation - matches the logical view of the program.

Question: Why is Banker's Algorithm important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It guarantees the system never enters a deadlock caused by resource allocation.

Definition: The Banker's algorithm is a deadlock avoidance method that grants a resource request only if the system stays in a safe state.

Example:
If granting a request leaves no safe sequence, the request is made to wait.

Question: Why is Inter-Process Communication (IPC) important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It enables cooperating processes and modular system design.

Definition: IPC is a set of mechanisms that let processes exchange data and coordinate their actions.

Example:
A shell uses a pipe to send the output of ls to grep.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Preemption?
Answer:
Limitation: It adds context-switch overhead and can cause problems such as race conditions on shared data.

Simple explanation: The OS interrupts a running process, often on a timer or when a higher-priority process arrives, and gives the CPU to another.

Example:
If a high-priority process becomes ready, the OS pauses the current one immediately.

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Process?
Answer:
Limitation: Processes are heavy: creating them and switching between them costs time and memory.

Simple explanation: A program is just a file on disk; when you run it, the OS creates a process with memory, a program counter and open files.

Example:
Opening Chrome twice creates two separate processes of the same program.

Question: In an interview, how would you explain Symbolic Link to a beginner?
Answer:
Definition: A symbolic (soft) link is a special file that points to another file or directory by its path.

Simple explanation: It works like a shortcut: opening it follows the path to the target.

Why it matters: It can link across file systems and to directories.

Example:
ln -s /data/file.txt link.txt creates a symbolic link.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Static linking vs Dynamic linking in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Static linking is copying library code into the executable at build time; Dynamic linking is linking shared libraries at run time.

Main differences:
- Size: Static linking - produces larger executables; Dynamic linking - produces smaller executables.
- Updates: Static linking - needs rebuilding to update libraries; Dynamic linking - updates the library separately.
- Dependencies: Static linking - is self-contained; Dynamic linking - depends on installed libraries.

Conclusion: Dynamic linking is more space-efficient, static linking is more portable.

Question: When would you choose Semaphore over Monitor?
Answer:

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Microkernel?

Example:
QNX and MINIX use a microkernel design.

Question: In an interview, how would you explain Operating System to a beginner?
Answer:

Simple explanation: It acts as a middleman between the user, applications and hardware, handling CPU time, memory, files and devices.

Why it matters: It makes the computer usable by hiding hardware complexity and sharing resources fairly and safely among programs.

Example:
Windows, Linux and macOS let you run many apps at once without each app managing the hardware itself.

Question: When would you choose Capability list over Access control list?

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Best fit vs Worst fit in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Best fit is choosing the smallest suitable hole; Worst fit is choosing the largest hole.

- Utilization: Best fit - is usually better; Worst fit - is usually worse.
- Search: Best fit - searches all holes; Worst fit - searches all holes.

Question: Which is better, Compaction or Paging?

Question: What is Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ) in an operating system?

Question: When would you choose Counting semaphore over Binary semaphore?

Question: What are the limitations or drawbacks of Booting?

Turning on a laptop leads to the login screen after the OS loads.

Question: Why is fork() System Call important in an operating system?

Question: Why is Process important in an operating system?

Question: When would you choose First fit over Best fit?

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Distributed OS vs Network OS in a few lines?

Question: What is the difference between Stack and Heap?

Question: Why is Swapping important in an operating system?

Question: When would you choose Non-blocking I/O over Blocking I/O?

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize API vs System call in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: API is a set of functions for programmers; System call is a direct request to the kernel.

- Level: API - is a higher level; System call - is a lower level.
- Portability: API - is more portable; System call - is OS-specific.

Question: Explain Spooling with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: Jobs are placed in a spool and the device processes them one by one at its own speed.

Several users print documents and the print spooler queues them for one printer.

Question: Why is Test-and-Set Instruction important in an operating system?

Question: When would you choose Swapping over Paging?

Question: Compare Linked allocation and Indexed allocation.

Question: When would you choose Page fault over Thrashing?
Answer:

Question: Compare Virtual machine and Container.
Answer:

Choose Virtual machine when you need different operating systems or strong isolation. Choose Container when you need fast, light deployment.

Question: Explain Direct Memory Access (DMA) with an example.

Question: What is Copy-on-Write (COW) in an operating system?

If the child only reads data, no copying ever happens.

Question: Which is better, Race condition or Deadlock?

Question: When would you choose Asynchronous I/O over Synchronous I/O?

Question: Compare System call and Library function.

Choose System call when you need OS services. Choose Library function when you want convenience.

Question: In an interview, how would you explain Thread to a beginner?

A web browser tab can use one thread for rendering and another for downloading a file.

Question: When would you choose Single-level directory over Multi-level directory?

Question: Which is better, Static linking or Dynamic linking?

Question: When would you choose Worst fit over Best fit?

Question: What is Symbolic Link in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: A symbolic (soft) link is a special file that points to another file or directory by its path.

Simple explanation: It works like a shortcut: opening it follows the path to the target.

Example:
ln -s /data/file.txt link.txt creates a symbolic link.

Question: Why is Convoy Effect important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: Understanding it explains why FCFS can give poor performance.

Definition: The convoy effect occurs when many short processes wait behind one long process.

Example:
One 100 ms job makes five 2 ms jobs wait 100 ms.

Question: When would you choose Multi-level directory over Single-level directory?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Multi-level directory when you have many files and users.

Simple explanation: Multi-level directory is a tree of directories. On organization, Multi-level directory - is good, whereas Single-level directory - is poor.

Example:
If you have many files and users, then Multi-level directory is the better fit than Single-level directory.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Sequential access vs Direct access in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Sequential access is reading a file from start to end; Direct access is jumping to any position in a file.

Main differences:
- Speed: Sequential access - is slow for random reads; Direct access - is fast for random reads.
- Use: Sequential access - suits logs and tapes; Direct access - suits databases.
- Simplicity: Sequential access - is simple; Direct access - needs positioning support.

Conclusion: Direct access is more flexible, and sequential suits streaming.

Question: When would you choose External fragmentation over Internal fragmentation?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose External fragmentation when you analyse segmentation or dynamic partitions.

Simple explanation: External fragmentation is free space scattered between allocated blocks. On cause, External fragmentation - is caused by variable-size allocation, whereas Internal fragmentation - is caused by fixed-size allocation.

Example:
If you analyse segmentation or dynamic partitions, then External fragmentation is the better fit than Internal fragmentation.

Question: What is Hold and Wait in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: Hold and wait is a deadlock condition where a process holds some resources while waiting for others.

Simple explanation: A process that already owns a resource requests more and blocks without releasing what it has.

Example:
P1 holds the printer while waiting for the scanner.

Question: What is the difference between Synchronous I/O and Asynchronous I/O?
Answer:
Short answer: Synchronous I/O is I/O where the caller waits for completion, while Asynchronous I/O is I/O where the caller continues while the operation runs.

Key differences:
- Waiting: Synchronous I/O - blocks the caller; Asynchronous I/O - does not block.
- Complexity: Synchronous I/O - is simple; Asynchronous I/O - is complex.
- Throughput: Synchronous I/O - has lower throughput; Asynchronous I/O - has higher throughput.

Question: Which is better, Preemptive kernel or Non-preemptive kernel?
Answer:
Verdict: Preemptive kernels are better for real-time work.

Simple explanation: Responsiveness: Preemptive kernel - is more responsive; Non-preemptive kernel - can have longer delays. Complexity: Preemptive kernel - is more complex; Non-preemptive kernel - is simpler.

Example:
Choose Preemptive kernel when you need low latency. Choose Non-preemptive kernel when you want simplicity.

Question: When would you choose Microkernel over Monolithic kernel?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Microkernel when you need security and modularity.

Simple explanation: Microkernel is a kernel with only the minimum services in kernel space. On size, Microkernel - is small, whereas Monolithic kernel - is large.

Example:
If you need security and modularity, then Microkernel is the better fit than Monolithic kernel.

Question: Which is better, Copy-on-write or Eager copying?
Answer:
Verdict: Copy-on-write is better in most cases.

Simple explanation: Speed: Copy-on-write - makes fork fast; Eager copying - makes fork slow. Memory: Copy-on-write - saves memory; Eager copying - uses more memory.

Example:
Choose Copy-on-write when child mostly reads. Choose Eager copying when child modifies most data.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize Process context switch vs Thread context switch in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: Process context switch is switching between processes; Thread context switch is switching between threads of the same process.

Main differences:
- Cost: Process context switch - is more expensive; Thread context switch - is cheaper.
- Memory: Process context switch - changes the address space; Thread context switch - keeps the same address space.
- TLB: Process context switch - may flush the TLB; Thread context switch - keeps TLB valid.

Conclusion: Thread switches are cheaper.

Question: When would you choose Pipe over Message queue?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Pipe when you connect related processes simply.

Simple explanation: Pipe is a one-way channel between processes. On direction, Pipe - is usually one-way, whereas Message queue - can be used both ways.

Example:
If you connect related processes simply, then Pipe is the better fit than Message queue.

Question: What is Kernel Thread in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: A kernel thread is a thread managed directly by the operating system kernel.

Simple explanation: The kernel schedules each thread separately, so blocked threads do not block the process.

Example:
Linux threads are implemented as kernel threads.

Question: Why is Process Synchronization important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It keeps shared data consistent.

Definition: Process synchronization is the coordination of concurrent processes so they access shared data safely.

Example:
Two threads updating a shared queue use a lock to avoid corrupting it.

Question: When would you choose Spooling over Buffering?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Spooling when many jobs share a slow device.

Simple explanation: Spooling is queuing jobs on disk for a device. On storage, Spooling - uses disk, whereas Buffering - uses RAM.

Example:
If many jobs share a slow device, then Spooling is the better fit than Buffering.

Question: Explain Container with an example.
Answer:
Simple explanation: The OS uses features such as namespaces and cgroups to isolate processes and limit resources.

Example:
Docker runs an application in a container with its libraries.

Key point: A container is a lightweight isolated environment that packages an application with its dependencies and shares the host kernel.

Question: What is Deadlock in an operating system?
Answer:
Definition: A deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are blocked forever, each waiting for a resource held by another.

Simple explanation: Each process holds a resource and waits for another one, so none can move forward.

Example:
P1 holds the printer and wants the scanner, while P2 holds the scanner and wants the printer.

Question: Why is Symbolic Link important in an operating system?
Answer:
Short answer: It can link across file systems and to directories.

Definition: A symbolic (soft) link is a special file that points to another file or directory by its path.

Example:
ln -s /data/file.txt link.txt creates a symbolic link.

Question: Compare Single-level directory and Multi-level directory.
Answer:
Definition: Single-level directory is one directory for all files. Multi-level directory is a tree of directories.

Simple explanation: They differ mainly in naming, organization and grouping. Naming: Single-level directory - requires unique names; Multi-level directory - allows same name in different directories.

Example:
Choose Single-level directory when you have few files. Choose Multi-level directory when you have many files and users.

Question: When would you choose Multilevel feedback queue over Multilevel queue?
Answer:
Short answer: Choose Multilevel feedback queue when behaviour changes over time.

Simple explanation: Multilevel feedback queue is a design with queues where processes can move. On flexibility, Multilevel feedback queue - is more flexible, whereas Multilevel queue - is less flexible.

Example:
If behaviour changes over time, then Multilevel feedback queue is the better fit than Multilevel queue.

Question: In an interview, how would you summarize DMA vs Programmed I/O in a few lines?
Answer:
One-line summary: DMA is data transfer without CPU involvement per byte; Programmed I/O is data transfer where the CPU moves every byte.

Main differences:
- CPU use: DMA - keeps the CPU free; Programmed I/O - keeps the CPU busy.
- Speed: DMA - is faster for large data; Programmed I/O - is slower.
- Hardware: DMA - needs a DMA controller; Programmed I/O - needs no extra hardware.

Conclusion: DMA is better for large transfers.

Question: Explain Hold and Wait with an example.
